I'm Salma, Shankar's classmate, and we share a study table in the library. The week after his girlfriend ended things, I expected him to vanish. Instead, on Monday, he showed me a sheet of paper.
'The next three weeks are going to be bad,' he said, very matter-of-fact. 'So I'm not going to trust my moods. I'm going to trust this.' The sheet said: classes, every one. Lunch at one with you lot. Bed by midnight, phone outside the room. And at the bottom, underlined: Nothing big gets decided on a bad day.
'Like what?' I asked.
'Like dropping the elective. Or shaving my head.' He almost smiled.
Some days he sat through lectures staring at nothing. But he came. Once he told me, 'Today's a bad day, so I'm not deciding about the internship till Friday.' I can't know how heavy it was inside, but by week four he was arguing with the professor again.

qa.q: What was underlined at the bottom of Shankar's sheet?
qa.a: Nothing big gets decided on a bad day.

qa.q: What does Shankar's matter-of-fact 'The next three weeks are going to be bad' suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt hurt and heavy but clear-headed enough to expect it, so he chose to rely on routine rather than his low moods.

qa.q: What else could Shankar add to the sheet for the hardest evenings?
qa.a: A name to call, like a friend or family member, so the evenings have some company as well as routine.

qa.q: How do those weeks look to Salma at the study table?
qa.a: Salma sees Shankar staring blankly some days but still turning up, and notices the old, argumentative Shankar return by week four.

grounding: Shows a student expecting the first weeks after a breakup to be heavy and planning around it with classes, meals, sleep and no big decisions on bad days.

Vaibhav, you've said no to every plan for three weeks. Let me, your Tejas mama, tell you what I did when I was twenty and my first relationship ended.
For four days I stayed in my hostel room and told everyone I had fever. Then my roommate Irfan knocked and wouldn't leave. So I told him, and my friend Suresh too. Just the two of them, the whole thing.
After that I made one rule: if someone invites me, I go, even if I sit in the corner. I went to a cricket match where I didn't watch a single ball. I went to Suresh's cousin's wedding and ate too much. And every Sunday I called my sister in Nagpur, even if I only said 'fine'.
It didn't make the pain go. It stopped it from growing in that small room.
So. There's a dinner at your aunt's on Saturday. You're coming with me.

qa.a: His roommate Irfan, and his friend Suresh too.

qa.q: How was Tejas feeling during the four days in the hostel room?

qa.a: Letting Irfan in and then making the rule to accept every invitation, even when not in the mood, which stopped the isolation.

qa.q: How might Irfan have seen those four days?
qa.a: Irfan likely sensed the fever story didn't add up and felt worried enough to knock and stay.

On the fourth evening she made herself message the two people she trusted most, her school friends Fiza and Anu, in a group chat: 'We broke up. I'm not okay.' Fiza called within five minutes.
She made a small plan after that. When the other interns asked her to biryani night on Friday, she said yes, though she wanted to say no. She sat quietly, but she laughed once. And she set a call with her brother Gautam in Bhubaneswar, every Sunday at seven.
On the third Sunday Gautam said, 'You sound more like yourself.' She did. The room still faced a wall, but the light was on.

In the reading room of the college library, Hafsa had her economics notes open and her phone under the table. Every ten minutes her thumb found its way to his profile. Still the same photo. Then a new one: him on a beach with friends, smiling.
She stared at it for a long time, looking for signs. Was he happy? Was the smile real? Did the girl on the left mean anything?
Afreen, across the table, slid over a note: 'You've been on the same page since 3.'
It was 5:20. Three weeks since the breakup, and each look made it feel like three hours. Every time she opened his page, it was like pressing a bruise to check it still hurt.
Later, in their hostel room, Hafsa admitted she'd looked at his profile maybe thirty times that day. 'I keep hoping I'll see something that tells me what to feel.'
'Does it ever?' Afreen asked.
Hafsa shook her head.

You asked on the phone why I still sound so low, two months after. I didn't know how to say it out loud, so I'm writing.

I'm Kishore, Chinmay's roommate. I noticed the changes before he explained them.
The first was his phone. The day after the breakup, I saw him scroll to her name, pause, and tap 'mute'. Not block. Just mute. He did the same on two other apps.
The second was his laptop. That evening he made a folder called 'Later' and dragged in every photo of the two of them, the Goa trip, the farewell party, the one on his desktop too. He replaced the background with plain blue.
The third surprised me. He started leaving ten minutes earlier for class, walking the long way round behind the canteen instead of past the girls' hostel.
When I asked, he said, 'I'm not angry at her. I just need less of her around for a while.'
I can't say how much it helped inside, but by the end of the month he was sleeping properly again.

qa.q: What did Chinmay name the folder of photos?
qa.a: 'Later'.

qa.q: What does 'I'm not angry at her. I just need less of her around' suggest about Chinmay?
qa.a: He still feels hurt but not bitter, and wants space to heal without any confrontation.

qa.q: What else could Chinmay add if reminders still catch him off guard?

Maria, you asked me how I got over my first big breakup. I'm Samir, I'm forty-five, and honestly, I didn't get over it for months. What helped was something my hostel warden made me do.
About six weeks after, I was still moping, and he handed me three sheets of paper. 'Write,' he said. 'What you valued. What didn't work. What you want next time.'
The first page was easy: she made me laugh, she pushed me to read. The second hurt: we never talked about money or family, we just avoided it, and I sulked instead of saying what I felt. The third was short: someone I can argue with kindly, and to be braver about hard talks myself.
I kept those sheets for twenty years. When I met your aunt, I read the third page again.

qa.q: What did the warden hand Samir?
qa.a: Three sheets of paper.

qa.q: How did Samir feel writing the second page?
qa.a: Samir felt hurt and a bit ashamed, admitting that hard topics were avoided and that sulking replaced saying what was felt.

qa.q: What choice in the story turned the moping into something useful?
qa.a: Accepting the warden's three sheets and writing honestly on each, which turned the pain into clear wishes for next time.

qa.q: How might the warden have seen Samir's moping?
qa.a: The warden likely noticed six weeks of moping and felt it was time for Samir to think, not just feel, so gave a simple task.

It had been seven weeks since Nazia ended things, and Tanvir had an exam in two days. The hostel corridor was loud with a birthday party. He couldn't study, and he couldn't stop thinking about her either.
So he gave himself twenty minutes. He took a page from his rough notebook and made three columns.
What I valued: her patience. How she noticed when I was tired. Our long walks after dinner.
What didn't work: I cancelled plans whenever my cricket team needed me. I never told her when something she said hurt; I went silent for days.
What I want next time: someone who likes walking as much as I do. And me, saying things out loud the same day.
When the twenty minutes ended, the party was still going. But his chest felt looser, and the second column no longer read like a list of her faults. Mostly it was his. He folded the page into his wallet and opened his notes.

subtype: Approach: seeking professional support when low persists [Revision]

The campus wellness centre had a fish tank and a box of tissues on every table. Aditi sat in the waiting room, knee bouncing, holding the appointment slip she'd booked online at midnight.
It had been two months since the breakup. She'd told herself it would pass. Instead she'd skipped nine classes, her mid-semester marks had dropped, and she felt heavy even on good days. Her friends had tried; she had stopped answering.
'Aditi?' A woman in a cotton sari smiled from a doorway. 'I'm Rukmini, one of the counsellors. Come in.'
Inside, Aditi said, 'I don't even know if this is serious enough to come here.'
'If you've felt this low since the breakup and your classes are suffering, that's reason enough,' Rukmini said. 'You don't have to wait until it's worse.'
They talked for fifty minutes. At the end, Aditi booked the next session for Thursday. Walking out, she felt, for the first time in weeks, that she wasn't carrying it alone.

qa.q: How many classes had Aditi skipped?
qa.a: Nine classes.

qa.q: What was Aditi feeling in the waiting room?
qa.a: She was nervous and unsure, her knee bouncing, and doubted whether her sadness was serious enough to bring there.

qa.a: Reply to one friend who tried to help and say she has started seeing a counsellor, so support comes from more than one place.

qa.a: Rukmini treats it as a common doubt and reassures Aditi that coming early is a good reason, not a failure.

I saw Megha at the food stalls. I knew she might be there, and I thought I was ready. I wasn't. She said 'hi' like nothing had happened, and I just stood there holding a paper plate of chaat, heart hammering. Then I mumbled something and walked straight into a pillar. Brilliant.
